title: Reading Documentation
tagline: Read any reference page, and turn what it says into code that works the first time
description: The skill under every other course: finding the right documentation and reading it precisely. How reference pages are laid out, reading C++ signatures, preconditions and undefined behaviour, cppreference and the standard library's return values, complexity and invalidation rules, Microsoft's Win32 pages with SAL annotations, error codes and versioned structures, Python, MDN and Node documentation, man pages, headers and specifications, and finally turning examples into robust code, checking your understanding with small experiments, coping with docs that are wrong, and writing documentation of your own. The practice has you implement functions exactly as documented, including every edge case. It assumes the C++ course up to classes.

milestones.title: How Reference Docs Work
milestones.blurb: The kinds of documentation and which one you need, the parts of a reference page, reading C++ signatures and overloads, and preconditions, guarantees and undefined behaviour.

lessons.title: Kinds of Documentation
lessons.summary: Why reading documentation is a core programming skill, the four kinds of documentation (tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation) and what each is for, the other sources you will meet, and how to pick the right one for the question you have.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Reference Page
lessons.summary: The sections nearly every reference page has - synopsis, description, parameters, return value, errors, complexity, notes, requirements, examples and see also - what each one tells you, and the order to read them in when you have a question.

lessons.title: Reading Signatures
lessons.summary: Decoding the declarations at the top of C++ reference pages - parameter and return types, const, references and pointers, default arguments, overload sets, templates and their named requirements, noexcept and [[nodiscard]] - so a signature tells you how to call a function before you read a word of prose.

lessons.title: Preconditions and Undefined Behaviour
lessons.summary: The contract a reference page describes - preconditions you must meet, what the function guarantees in return, what happens on failure - half-open ranges, the difference between checked and unchecked functions, exception guarantees, and why "the behaviour is undefined" is the most important sentence on a page.

projects.title: A string library built from its reference

milestones.title: The C++ Standard Library Reference
milestones.blurb: Finding your way around cppreference, how standard functions report results and errors, complexity and iterator invalidation, and which C++ version a feature needs.

lessons.title: Finding Your Way Around cppreference
lessons.summary: How cppreference.com is organised - by header and by topic - the layout of a class page with its member tables and version markers, what a function page adds (possible implementation, defect reports, examples), how it relates to the C++ standard, and fast ways to land on the right page.

tasks.title: Two ways to read a number

lessons.title: Return Values and Error Reporting
lessons.summary: The many ways standard library functions report their results - end iterators, npos, pairs with a bool, optional, error codes, exceptions and the paired throwing and non-throwing overloads of std::filesystem - and how to read each from the reference page and handle it correctly.

lessons.title: Complexity and Invalidation
lessons.summary: Two promises every container page makes - how cost grows (constant, amortised constant, logarithmic, linear) and which iterators, pointers and references stay valid after each operation - how to read the invalidation rules, and the bugs that come from ignoring them.

lessons.title: Versions and Feature Tests
lessons.summary: Making sure what you read applies to what you compile - version markers on reference pages, choosing the language standard with /std and -std, compiler support tables, __cplusplus and _MSVC_LANG, feature-test macros from the version header, deprecated and removed features, and reading the std::format specification as an example of a C++20 feature.

projects.title: The four ways to put into a map
A vector built to its specification

milestones.title: Windows Documentation
milestones.blurb: A Win32 reference page from top to bottom, SAL annotations and buffer sizes, GetLastError, HRESULT and NTSTATUS, and structures, flags and versions.

lessons.title: A Win32 Reference Page
lessons.summary: Reading a Microsoft Learn page for a Windows API function from top to bottom - the syntax block and its types, parameter directions, the exact wording of the return value, the remarks where the surprises live, and the requirements table with header, library, DLL and minimum Windows version - using GetModuleFileNameW as the example.

lessons.title: SAL Annotations and Buffer Sizes
lessons.summary: The source annotation language in Windows headers - _In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _opt_, _Out_writes_ and friends - what each promises about a parameter, characters versus bytes, and the three patterns Windows uses for buffers whose size you do not know in advance.

tasks.title: Ask for the size, then fetch

lessons.title: GetLastError, HRESULT and NTSTATUS
lessons.summary: The three error systems you meet in Windows documentation - the per-thread last error, COM's HRESULT with its severity, facility and code bits, and the kernel's NTSTATUS - how a page tells you which one a function uses, how to decode each, and how to turn them into readable messages.

lessons.title: Structures, Flags and Versions
lessons.summary: Reading the parts of Windows pages that describe data - structures whose first member gives their size, reserved fields, zero-initialisation, flag parameters that combine with OR versus parameters that take one value, mutually exclusive flags, and version requirements and _WIN32_WINNT.

projects.title: A registry-style API built to its documentation

milestones.title: Other Languages and Specifications
milestones.blurb: Python's documentation, MDN and Node for JavaScript, reading headers and source code when the docs fall short, and man pages, RFCs and specifications.

lessons.title: Python's Documentation
lessons.summary: Finding and reading docs.python.org - the tutorial, library reference and language reference - Python signature notation with defaults, / and *, the version notes that say when behaviour changed, how a page describes exceptions, and help(), docstrings and type stubs from inside Python.

lessons.title: JavaScript, MDN and Node
lessons.summary: Reading MDN Web Docs - syntax lines with optional parameters, return values and exceptions, the specification links and the browser compatibility tables - the ECMAScript specification behind them, and Node.js documentation with its stability index, callback and promise signatures and error codes.

lessons.title: Reading Headers and Source Code
lessons.summary: What to do when the documentation is thin or missing - reading a library's header for its real declarations, defaults and doc comments, Doxygen tags, finding the implementation with Go to Definition, using a project's tests as examples, and reading the source of the standard library itself.

tasks.title: Using a library from its header

lessons.title: Man Pages, RFCs and Specifications
lessons.summary: Reading the most precise documents you will meet - Unix man pages with their sections and ERRORS lists, RFCs with the MUST, SHOULD and MAY keywords of RFC 2119, ABNF grammars, errata, and turning one section of a specification into code and tests.

milestones.title: From Docs to Working Code
milestones.blurb: Turning an example into robust code, checking your understanding with small experiments, what to do when the docs are wrong or missing, and writing documentation others can use.

lessons.title: Turning an Example into Your Code
lessons.summary: Why documentation examples are not production code - what they leave out on purpose - and a dependable routine for adapting one - run it unchanged, understand every line against the reference, make it a function, add every error path the reference describes, release resources on every path, and test the edges.

lessons.title: Checking Your Understanding with Experiments
lessons.summary: Confirming what you think a page says with small, focused programs - one question per experiment, predicting the result first, trying the edge cases, using Compiler Explorer, turning experiments into learning tests that keep checking the behaviour - and the limits of experiments when behaviour is undefined or unspecified.

lessons.title: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
lessons.summary: What to do when documentation and behaviour disagree - checking the version first, reading changelogs and migration guides, errata and known issues, weighing community answers and AI suggestions, reporting documentation bugs well, and protecting your code against behaviour that is not documented.

tasks.title: A migration written from a changelog

lessons.title: Writing Documentation Others Can Use
lessons.summary: Turning everything this course taught about reading documentation into writing it - doc comments that state the contract, what every function's documentation must answer, examples that are correct, READMEs that get someone started, changelogs, and keeping documentation true as the code changes.

tasks.title: Reading doc comments with a program
